explanation: Fires on the last token before a clause's predicate (a modal or auxiliary such as 'will', "'ll", 'would', 'could', the infinitival 'to', or the subject pronoun immediately before a verb) when the clause predicates an experience, benefit or need of a person: the addressee or speaker ('you', 'I', 'we', imperatives, if-clauses), an indefinite class of people placed under a condition ('visitors who arrive before noon will...', 'ticket holders who were affected will be entitled to...'), or a fixed evaluative or perception frame aimed at the reader ('it was no uncommon sight to see', 'great to hear that', 'again, in Isaias, we read'). Strength follows how much of that person-facing set-up has already been read and how prospective it is, never the verb that follows: 'will' with a condition clause inside the subject (12.2), an if/imperative offer ('if you arrive before noon, you will', 11.2; 'sign up to receive', 11.2) or a cited-source reading ('again, in Isaias, we read', 9.8) is strong, while bare 'X will receive' with no condition (2.9), present-tense, past-tense or 'can' description of a definite third party in a scene ('each received' 1.3, 'are receiving' 2.2, 'each visitor is given' 3.5, 'visitors can also see' 1.8) and agentive clauses ('the charity will give...' 0.9) stay under 6; the verb after the peak is inert (an object swap leaves the peak identical), and an inanimate subject fires only inside a running benefaction list ('the roads that will be repaired ... will each benefit from £58,000', 26.0).
